The syntax is horrible.

Subjective, of course. JavaScript uses many of the same syntactic constructs that Java uses, which were adopted from C. In particular, to reference a field inside a data structure, you use the dot operator (or arrow if the field is a pointer you want to dereference). Example:

 struct s {
 int field;
 int* pfield;
 };

 int d=s.field;
 d=s->pfield;

Java does away with pointer arithmetic, and instead of structs you have subclasses of Object, leading to statements like these:

 System.out.println(new StringBuffer("e")+(new Int(1337).toString()));

In this example, you would not need to write the StringBuffer constructor explicitly, it will be called anyway.

Other object-oriented languages have more readable syntax like this valid inform program:

 print "e" , 1337

JavaScript is a functional language, not an object-oriented one, but adopts the same notations. As an example 

 console.log('e'+parseInt('1337',10))

Granted, this is a bit convoluted. This also works:

 console.log('e'+1337)

The equivalent CoffeeScript code looks like this:

 console.log "e" + 1337

Here is another example for a JavaScript function:

ack = function (m,n) {
 if(n==0){return m+1
 }else if(m==0){return ack(n-1,1)
 }else{return ack(n-1,ack(n,m-1))
 }
}

The equivalent CoffeeScript code looks like this:

 ack = (m, n) ->
 if m is 0 then n + 1
 else if m > 0 and n is 0 then ack m - 1, 1
 else ack m - 1, ack m, n - 1

And the equivalent Haskell (also a functional language) looks like this:

 ack 0 n = n+1
 ack m 0 = ack (m-1) 1
 ack m n = ack (m-1) (ack m (n-1))

The type system, or lack thereof, is horrible.

This is objectively true. JavaScript does have types, and implicitly converts between them. Declaring types is not possible. Any data structures defined by the programmer can not be declared their own type, but are implicitly converted on demand. The typeof operator, which returns a string object of the name of the type of its parameter, rarely returns something useful. For example, an array of anything is simply of type "object", which is equivalent to any other object in boolean contexts, even using the comparison operators that don't implicitly convert types.

Some mechanical engineers I know are rather fond of typeless languages, and happily hack away in MatLab, multiplying polynomials with complex matrices, using the results as strings.

But in a language where

 alert(array(16).join({}-1)+' Gary')

is valid code, it is quite difficult to prove that what your program does can not possibly be what you intended to do.

JavaScript's excuse for a type system is worse than no type system at all. Tcl has no types, because everything is a unicode string, which in some contexts is a list, and in others what ticklers call an array (but in most other languages is called a dictionary or a hashmap, except in JavaScript where it is a table), and sometimes a number, but everything is always a string. In JavaScript, you can't be sure what anything is, even when you use the typeof operator, which in most cases just tells you something is an object, but not if that object is a function, an array, or null. There are special comparison operators that don't convert the type, so you know that "0" and 0 are not equal, unless you implicitly convert the type for comparison, and then boolean equivalence is not transitive.

I don't want or need a Turing-complete language in my documents. It is a solution in search of a problem. It is a security nightmare.

JavaScript does make it possible to verify form data before it is submitted, giving instant feedback to the user. The same could be achieved with regular expressions. The submitted data has to be verified again by the server backend, meaning it has to be done twice, and unless the backend is written in node, using different code in a different language using different syntax, making it difficult to guarantee that both systems accept the same input (especially when the server backend is written in PHP).

JavaScript also makes it possible to re-write the entire document it is embedded in, or even generate it. It can do so not only by manipulating the document object model tree, but also by injecting random text and evaluating it.

document.write('<script>document.body.appendChild(document.createTextNode("<style type=\"text/css\">body visibility:hidden</style>"))</script>')

This injected text can also contain scripts to be evaluated. That seems cool, but keep in mind that except for contrieved cases that code is multiple times as much data as the document it generates - and that that code can change at runtime, through unsanitized input or rogue external dependencies. (Which, again, may sound cool if you only think what you could do with that, until you deliver and suddenly have to think about what others could do with that.)

JavaScript is not limited to manipulating the document, but also the user agent (i.e. the browser) by resizing its window, spawning new windows (like alert boxes), opening new documents (in new windows or replacing the current content), loading documents and code, and even submitting form data, causing denial-of-service, out-of-memory conditions, and fork-bombing the host system.

And for convenience, JavaScript can read you browser history without you noticing, and transmit it in the background.

Performance should not even matter, yet somehow it is crucial.

Originally, JavaScript was an interpreted language. It was not expected to do much beyond manipulating documents. Documents, including HTML documents, are expected to be rather static, and not change much subject to user input. These days, entire user applications are written in JavaScript, meaning that browsers do not only display documents, but are a platform for general-purpose programming, including entire office suites. Some websites are no longer repositories of data, but repositories of code. Facebook delivers around 50_000 lines of code to be executed each time a user agent connects to the site, generating not a document, but several user interfaces (which contain no URIs). It is the reason JavaScript had to be compiled before execution, paving the way for more complex applications, because interpreting the code continuously would be too slow.

Unfortunately, as explained above, there is no way to optimize JavaScript code for performance through a compiler because data is converted on the fly for any new function that might appear. JS.ASM uses syntactic tricks to guarantee some type safety in at least some contexts, allowing for some optimization, but the syntax is even more awkward and less readable than JavaScript is already.

[++[+[]][+[]]]+[+[]]-[++[+[]][+[]]]

I am the creator of this forum and the one who sent out the flyers. I purchased a place in Union Square a bit over a year ago. Moving into a completely empty condo, I felt myself really wanting for some kind of(even physical) bulletin board. There's constantly people moving out/in and I thought how useful it would be if we could easily communicate with each other and perhaps purchase huge heavy items from people in the complex rather than having to travel and transport or buy them at full price at a local retail store. I've worked my ass off putting together furniture I ordered online and coordinating transportation for things purchased elsewhere - it wasn't fun.

During my short time here, I have witnessed a big scandal with people's packages being stolen when left outside the door. I personally wasn't a victim but I have heard that incidents were very prevalent. I have also encountered quite a few events that I wished I had the ability to reach out to my neighbours and notify them of, for all of our mutual benefit. My hope is that everyone living in this community can join this forum and have a full and open communication network between neighbours.
